I analyzed Texas (TxDOT) bid data for 4,583 projects. Here's what I found.  Hey all, I've been poking around public bid data lately, and figured you might find some of it interesting. Pulled the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) bid tabulation dataset: 732,235 18,171 bids (see edit 2) across 4,583 projects from Jan 2024 through now. Here's what jumped out. Win rates: For contractors with 10+ bids on record: - Median win rate: 23.2% - 44.2% of contractors win less than 1 in 5 - Only 20.2% win more than half their bids So if you're hitting 20-25%, you're right at the median. Better than nearly half the field. This is the interesting part. Of all losing bids 83,292 lost by 5% or less. That burns!: | Gap to Winner | % of Losses | Raw Count | | ≤1% | 3.0% | 17,195 bids | | ≤5% | 14.8% | 83,292 bids | | ≤10% | 29.3% | 165,387 bids | The median loss margin was 17.7% so half of all losses were closer than that, half were further. The distribution has a long tail of people who missed by a lot, but a solid chunk are in the ballpark. Competition varies by district Average bidders per project overall: 4.0 Most competitive districts: - Childress: 5.1 avg bidders (57 projects) - Tyler: 4.9 avg bidders (137 projects) - Yoakum: 4.8 avg bidders (256 projects) Least competitive: - Lubbock: 3.3 avg bidders (122 projects) - Maintenance Division: 3.3 avg bidders (38 projects) - Laredo: 3.2 avg bidders (93 projects) 8.7% of projects only had one bidder. Location matters. Seasonality - Busiest: Aug - Slowest: Dec Bid spreads are all over the place On projects with 3+ bidders, the median spread (low to high) was 44.5%. Only 5.6% of projects had spreads under 10%. So there's real variance out there, some sees everyone's within a few percent, others have wildly different reads on scope/risk. Data's public on data.texas.gov if anyone wants to dig in themselves. Happy to answer questions. Since this is Texas-only. I might do the same type of analysis for other states if I have time/there is interest. Do these data make sense to you? I was quite surprised by the number of close losses. EDIT: A commenter pointed out that mixing maintenance with construction projects skews the data. They were right: | Metric | Construction | Maintenance | | Median Win Rate | 17.2% | 24.3% | | Median Bid Spread | 40.0% | 51.1% | | Losses ≤ 5%| 15.7% | 10.6% | Construction is indeed tighter. EDIT 2: Thanks to another commenter I noticed that there is a mistake: the 732,235 number is the total row count of the dataset, not the unique bid count. TxDOT data lists every single line item (mobilization, asphalt, traffic control, etc.) as a separate row. The correct number of bids is 18,171, I will add this correction in the edit. The good news is that the "4.0 average bidders" and the win/loss percentages in the post were calculated using unique vendor IDs per project, so those stats hold up.

The title : Estimator  I don’t usually jump into the “thought-provoking posts” world, in fact, this might be my first attempt. But earlier today I spotted a recruiter advertising for a Pre-Construction Cost Engineer… and the job description read almost exactly like what most of us would call an Estimator. And it got me thinking… With how the role has evolved, is the title “Estimator” still doing the job justice? These days, an Estimator’s work is so much more than counting fittings or measuring pipework. We’re brought in earlier than ever. We collaborate with design teams, project teams, suppliers, and subcontractors. We identify risks before they become problems. We shape solutions, not just price them. We often get asked for GMP or a fixed-price lump sum. At that point we are not “estimating” anymore. We are effectively committing. We are taking on risk, validating scope, clarifying design gaps, interrogating supply chains, sense-checking programmes, and then putting our name (and margin) on a number that we will be expected to stand by. We don’t simply estimate, we analyse, we challenge, we guide, and we influence outcomes. So maybe it is time the role had a new name? I’d love to hear what others in the profession think.

Is BIM or PDF + AI the future of preconstruction?  Hey it’s been 4 years since I posted this thread wondering if we’d ever see estimating directly from a Revit model (https://www.reddit.com/r/architecture/comments/pu3amf/will_estimating_and_bidding_from_a_revit_model/). Back then, I was running the tech team at a facade fabrication company and was exploring how BIM could help us better provide design assistance to architects, automate aspects of estimating or at least budget pricing, and all the other supposed benefits of BIM (the industry’s favorite buzzword before AI) A lot has changed since then – ChatGPT, LLMs, Multi-modal AI. As a tech guy, the dream has always been that software can enable better collaboration & efficiency for projects. Buildings are so complex that you divide up the work between 100 companies, yet so much of this coordination happens manually via PDF with very little automation. I think there’s 2 general paths for tech progress in the industry: BIM-centric: In this path, the BIM model should serve as the hub of info throughout the project lifecycle. If there’s an actual 3D model of the building to a sufficient level of detail and associated data for each element, that could make so many processes more efficient: material takeoffs would be a simple button click Can Revit move from just being a tool architects/engineers use to generate the construction document PDFs? As projects advance, the model would get more detailed, edited like a Google Doc by the different domain experts In my opinion, the main issues with this path are incentives, industry fragmentation, legal, and construction realities. It costs time & expertise to model things in Revit – even if we assume the benefits outweigh the costs, who pays for this? The legal architect deliverables are the PDF drawings/specs. A BIM model would require lots of rules around level of detail and responsibility Some things like key dimensions are just simply not known until construction has started with multiple layers of human/material deviations. Existing PDF workflows + AI on top: The alternative approach is to keep with what we’re doing now and layer on the latest AI models to become more efficient Instead of using a BIM model to get the facade panel takeoff, we could have AI read through the PDF elevations, floor plans, and details to generate this. This example is only partially possible today: while you might be able to get AI to count panels on a simple facade with perfect annotations, it probably can’t interpret “design intent”. However, AI is getting much better and the latest reasoning + multimodal models have opened up some new capabilities There’s potentially smaller things AI could do like: Scope Analysis - while AI can’t perform takeoffs of facade panels, you can know which elevations have which materials/components/etc. With some training, you can have it associate details/sections with elevations and figure out where subtle window jamb panels are or if there's corner closures Spec vs Drawing Conflicts - AI can read through and create an internal representation of scope items, then cross check requirements between specs and drawings (or within drawings) to find conflicts Bid leveling - read PDF bids to understand what each one offers/excludes and create a custom excel spreadsheet to level them New types of productivity/PM tools – AI is great at reading project emails, can keep track of tasks, extract structured data, create detailed status updates. Basically help do some of the admin work on a project The benefit of this path is you can experiment with the rapidly-changing AI models and adopt tools if they work without needing other companies to change. If you can split your workflows into small pieces, the existing AI models are actually quite capable with some prompt engineering, software development, or fine-tuning Curious what others think, which path will be better (or neither)? Building a community of people interested in these types of ideas If you’ve made it this far, you’re probably interested in tech. I’m looking to build a small group of industry professionals that want to explore the latest AI reasoning models or BIM workflows in construction, very informal and hands-on experimenting. Feel free to comment or DM me if you’re interested.

Training for Estimating Newcomers  I've been a professional estimator for over 15 years, working on both the owner and GC sides. During that time, I’ve trained around two dozen people in the basics—usually interns, associate-level staff, or even site guys who’ve moved up to SI and need to know how to perform basic take-offs. In my experience, only about 50% of people truly "get" estimating. They might understand the process and the expected outcomes on the surface, but something doesn’t quite click. They struggle to apply logical, methodical thinking to the work. For those who don’t get it, there’s often a mix of fear, avoidance, and a tendency to produce chaotic results. No matter how many times I review their work or guide them, the same mistakes persist. This isn’t to insult anyone’s intelligence or capabilities. I’ve seen incredibly sharp college graduates fail to grasp, while others with a GED—people I wasn’t even sure could dress themselves properly—have created some of the most precise spreadsheets I’ve ever seen. I do wonder if my expectations are unreasonable after so many years of doing estimates myself. I’ve developed a baseline that might be hard for others to meet, but I can’t shake the feeling that I’m missing something in how I approach training. Recently, I had to let someone go after a year because she just couldn’t produce the necessary work and I felt a bit of personal failure over it. I had reviewed the process for takeoffs, explained what to look for and what to deliver, but despite my efforts, she wasn’t able to complete the tasks successfully. My usual training process involves walking new hires through the high-level steps of an estimate, using real examples from estimates I’ve prepared along with supporting drawings and documentation. Afterward, I have them work on a smaller project, then review their process and results together. I try to be patient and open, encouraging questions and providing constructive feedback. I make a point of avoiding the harsh, condescending approach of the person who trained me—someone who would suggest I was incompetent and might be fired every time I asked a question. That said, I’m open to suggestions. Does anyone have training methods that work particularly well for them? I know everyone learns differently, and I’m eager to improve my approach. If you’ve found something that helps people better understand the estimating process, I’d love to hear about it.

An in-depth guide for finding subs in 24-hrs  Hello construction reddit, I see a lot of posts from GCs asking “how do I find subs to bid?”. This is especially hard for GCs that are moving to new markets because they have no existing relationships (e.g. traveling GC that is expanding operations from CA to NV). A lot of posts & blogs provide generic strategies like Use google maps Use bid platforms like building connected, smartbid Drive around in a truck and talk to subs Ask for referrals IMO these solutions are surface-level and don’t truly solve the problem. A few months ago, I saw an opportunity to build sublists quickly using techniques common in the software industry (web-scraping, programmatic emailing, machine learning) and it’s been working well. Today, I want to share insights on how to build sublists with the community because it might be useful to other GCs. Background For context, I built company that makes bid-management tools for commercial trade contractors. We have a sales team that needs high-quality commercial subcontractor leads. Sourcing these leads proved difficult. We scraped databases (BlueBook, BuildingConnected), but we ran into so many data problems (subs in wrong trades, wrong contact info) We’d use google maps, but half the results were residential leads and useless for us We’d purchase lists from companies like ZoomInfo, but they missed a lot of important construction-specific attributes that sales needed (e.g. trade, union/non-union) So we built an in-house solution to generate sublists quickly. Then one day, a GC friend saw this and asked if he could use this for one of his projects. He’s the chief estimator GC that builds luxury retail chains (Tiffany’s, Dior, Ralph Lauren) and they travel all over the country. It turns out it’s critical for them to build high-quality sublists quickly in new territories as well. He inspired me to write this post b/c he found our tool useful. Problem Let’s say you’re a GC that focuses on luxury retail work in Los Angeles, CA, but you’ve won a negotiated job in Las Vegas, NV. How would you generate a list of NV subs that would be a good fit for the job? Our goal was to generate a list of subs with this information Trades performed Area of work MWBE status Union / non-union status Average project size Past projects Estimating decision makers (emails & phone #s) Failed Solutions We tried a lot of methods, but they all failed for different reasons. Google maps + calls Using google maps, we would run a query “electrical contractors in Las Vegas”, then research their website and manually call each sub to ask if they had done luxury retail. The problem is it took days and hours just to prep a sublist. As a small estimating team we didn’t have the manpower to call the thousands of subs and vet them. BuildingConnected & Planhub & other bid platforms BuildingConnected & Planhub seemed like a nice solution because they have a large database of subs. We ran into two problems. First, the information was out-of-date (subs listed under wrong trades, contact information was wrong) which caused us to have to manually fix a lot of the data. Secondly, we’d send a generic ITB and barely get any responses because in any competitive market, subs don’t respond to generic bid-platform ITBs. Ask for referrals We’d ask for referrals from 1-2 local subs and then slowly work the network. For example, we’d talk to a manufacturer’s rep, get 1-3 HVAC subs. Then we’d ask these HVAC subs for recs for drywall and electrical and glass subs, rinse and repeat. This was great, but it was still incredibly time-consuming. Again manpower issue. Our approach (web-scraping, machine learning, programmatic emails) The definition of a great sublist is simple. Find every single subcontractor in an area Get accurate, up-to-date on the sub (e.g. trades performed, MWBE, union/non-union) Find the right decision maker My challenge was to build a way so that our estimating team could push a button and get accurate sublists without doing any work. The first thing I did was break down this challenge into mini-problems. (A) Map the universe of subs in an area The first challenge was to find every single construction sub in a market. To do that, I built a web-scraper that would pull a sub’s name and website URL from a few construction databases, which publicly list subs. BlueBook Association websites for specialty trades like NECA, AWCI In addition, google maps has an API so you can run automated queries like “electrical sub in <zip code>”. I created a list of common trades we needed and every zip code in the nation to build a gigantic list of subs. If a sub had a website or some internet presence, these methods would find it. Now I have a gigantic list of every sub in the U.S. (B) Scrape each website, clean the data & get accurate information about the sub A gigantic list of subs and websites isn’t useful and there’s a lot of problems. For example, the sub’s website may be out-of-date, it may be a manufacturer’s rep rather than a sub. Therefore, the second challenge was to clean the data and make it useful for bidding outreach. To do that, I built a web-scraping tool that would visit website-by-website and extract the following information Trades performed Area of work MWBE status Union / non-union status Average project size Past projects Estimating decision makers (emails & phone #s) Phone #s Estimating email Here are some examples of the techniques i used Predict the trade based on the description on the home-page using machine learning (e.g. if the word electrical is common on a home-page, predict that it’s an electrical sub) Extract basic info (e.g. location, emails, phone numbers) using web-scraping Look for specific keywords like MWBE, union using web-scraping The output is a clean excel sheet with every sub in our market, enriched with key information. (C) Get contact information Armed with a clean sublist, the next challenge was to find the decision maker at each company and his or her contact information. Unfortunately, most websites don’t list the chief estimator’s contact information and just have generic emails like [info@subcontractor.com](mailto:info@subcontractor.com). In our experience, if you just blindly send a bid to a generic email you’ll never get a response. To start, I used a tool called phantom buster which would allow me to extract employee and job-titles from a company’s linkedin. Then I used a software script to guess each person’s email and use third-party email verification to confirm the email is correct. By using this process, we now had direct contacts at each company and their email. (D) Fill in the data gaps with programmatic emails However, not everyone in construction is on linkedin, let alone chief estimators. So for the companies where we didn’t find the right estimating decision maker, we would directly email a contact at the company with a templated email asking for the decision maker. In this email, I would add a bit of salesmanship (introduce myself, introduce the project and the estimated revenue). Most people would manually write every email, but we used tools like Lemlist that basically allow you to send a personal-email from your domain, but do this in a programmatic way. This allows you to email 100s of companies simultaneously. We gathered these responses and added it to our list of contacts. For the companies that never responded, we’d directly call and ask for the decision maker. Impact for GC friend In summary, we built a tool that breaks down generating sublists into a few components. Finding all subs Vetting subs programmatically using their website Finding up-to-date contact info for these subs Reaching out via emails & calls for info that we’re missing Per my GC friend, this tool has given them a way to generate fast-sublists so they can be more strategic about getting bid coverage since they’re no longer blindly calling every sub, but just prioritizing the ones that are a good fit using the data we’ve scraped. For the GCs, I’m curious to hear how you guys generate sublists at your company because I’m looking to improve this tool.
